WITH charged AS (                      -- only succeeded generations use credits
  SELECT gen_id, account_id, created_ts, credits,
         date_trunc('month', created_ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS month
  FROM generations
  WHERE status = 'succeeded'
), running AS (
  SELECT c.*,
         SUM(credits) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id, month
                            ORDER BY created_ts, gen_id
                            ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS used_so_far
  FROM charged c
), account_months AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT account_id, month FROM charged
), allowance AS (                      -- the plan in effect at the month's first instant
  SELECT am.account_id, am.month, p.monthly_credits AS allowance
  FROM account_months am
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT pc.plan
    FROM plan_changes pc
    WHERE pc.account_id = am.account_id
      AND pc.effective_ts < (am.month + INTERVAL '1 month') AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'
    ORDER BY (pc.effective_ts <= am.month::timestamp AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') DESC,  -- at or before the start first
             CASE WHEN pc.effective_ts <= am.month::timestamp AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'
                  THEN pc.effective_ts END DESC,                                -- the latest of those
             pc.effective_ts                                                    -- else the first in the month
    LIMIT 1
  ) pl
  JOIN plans p ON p.plan = pl.plan
)
SELECT r.account_id, r.month, a.allowance,
       COUNT(*)            AS charged_generations,
       SUM(r.credits)      AS credits_used,
       (ARRAY_AGG(r.gen_id ORDER BY r.created_ts, r.gen_id)
          FILTER (WHERE r.used_so_far >= a.allowance))[1] AS ran_out_gen,
       MIN(r.created_ts) FILTER (WHERE r.used_so_far >= a.allowance) AS ran_out_at
FROM running r
JOIN allowance a ON a.account_id = r.account_id AND a.month = r.month
GROUP BY r.account_id, r.month, a.allowance
ORDER BY r.month, r.account_id;

Explanation. Failed generations are removed first, so they neither add credits nor create rows. The running total is per account and UTC month, ordered by (created_ts, gen_id) with an explicit ROWS frame: with the default RANGE frame two generations at the same second get the same total, and the first of them would be reported as the one that ran out even when it alone did not reach the allowance. The allowance is an as-of lookup: the latest plan change at or before the month's first instant, or, for an account created during the month, its first plan. Because the running total only grows, the generation that ran out is the first row whose total is at least the allowance; ARRAY_AGG(… ORDER BY …)[1] picks it by time, not by id (ids are not in time order in the data).

Complexity. One sort of the charged generations by (account_id, month, created_ts, gen_id) for the window, a hash aggregate, and one small index-friendly lookup per account-month for the plan: O(n log n). An index on plan_changes (account_id, effective_ts) makes the lateral lookup a seek.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_ts), MONTH); ARRAY_AGG(gen_id IGNORE NULLS ORDER BY created_ts, gen_id LIMIT 1)[OFFSET(0)] with IF(...) instead of FILTER; no LATERAL, so rank plan changes with ROW_NUMBER() in a join. Snowflake: MIN_BY(gen_id, created_ts) does not break ties by gen_id, so use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() over qualifying rows; ASOF JOIN exists for the plan lookup. Spark SQL: min_by on a struct (created_ts, gen_id); window frames are ROWS only when written. MySQL 8: no FILTER (use CASE), no arrays; take the first qualifying row with ROW_NUMBER().

Edge cases built into the data. An account whose running total reaches the allowance exactly; one that never reaches it; an account-month with only failed generations (no row); failed generations interleaved with charged ones; gen_ids not in time order. Hard: two months with generations in the last minute of September and the first minute of October; two generations of one account at the same second where neither alone reaches the allowance but together they do. Very Hard: a plan upgrade mid-September (September keeps the old allowance), a change exactly at 2026-10-01 00:00:00 (October uses it), an account created mid-September, and accounts.plan holding only the current plan.

Counting failed generations; > instead of >=; the default RANGE frame or ordering by created_ts alone; MIN(gen_id) for the generation; months in the session's or a local time zone; joining accounts.plan for every month; an inner join to a plan lookup that drops the account created mid-month.

WITH new_users AS (                    -- a user is new to an app once: at their first install
  SELECT user_id, app, MIN(installed_ts) AS first_ts
  FROM installs
  GROUP BY user_id, app
), flagged AS (
  SELECT n.app,
         date_trunc('month', n.first_ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS cohort_month,
         n.first_ts + INTERVAL '7 days' <= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}' AS measurable,
         EXISTS (
           SELECT 1 FROM saves s
           WHERE s.user_id = n.user_id AND s.app = n.app
             AND s.location = 'cloud'
             AND s.saved_ts >= n.first_ts
             AND s.saved_ts <  n.first_ts + INTERVAL '7 days'
         ) AS saved_in_week
  FROM new_users n
)
SELECT app, cohort_month,
       COUNT(*)                                            AS new_users,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE measurable)                  AS measurable_users,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE measurable AND saved_in_week) AS activated,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE measurable AND saved_in_week)::numeric
             / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE measurable), 0), 4) AS activation_rate
FROM flagged
GROUP BY app, cohort_month
ORDER BY app, cohort_month;

Explanation. MIN(installed_ts) per user and app defines the cohort and removes reinstalls in one step. The activation test is a semi-join (EXISTS) to cloud saves of the same app in the half-open window [first, first + 7 days), so several saves cannot multiply rows. Measurability is a right-censoring rule: a user whose seven days are not over by as_of cannot yet be classified, so they are kept out of both numerator and denominator; counting them as "not activated" biases the most recent cohort down, and counting only the ones who already saved biases it up. NULLIF makes a cohort with nobody measurable report NULL rather than fail.

Complexity. One aggregate over installs and an indexed probe per new user into saves (user_id, app, saved_ts): O(n log n) with that index, a hash semi-join otherwise.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: TIMESTAMP_ADD(first_ts, INTERVAL 7 DAY), COUNTIF, SAFE_DIVIDE, DATE_TRUNC(DATE(first_ts), MONTH). Snowflake: DATEADD(day, 7, first_ts), COUNT_IF, DIV0NULL is not the same as NULL (it returns 0), so keep NULLIF. Spark SQL: first_ts + INTERVAL 7 DAYS, count_if, EXISTS subqueries are supported; trunc(first_ts, 'MM'). MySQL 8: DATE_ADD, SUM(CASE …), DATE_FORMAT(first_ts, '%Y-%m-01').

Edge cases built into the data. A reinstall more than a week after the first install followed by a cloud save (not activated, not a new user again); a save exactly 7 days after the first install; a save in another app; users with several saves; a user with no saves. Hard: local saves inside the window; a save at the install instant; a first install in the last minute of September; a user new to two apps. Very Hard: as_of a few days into November, a user whose window ends exactly at as_of (measurable), users installed within the last 7 days (some already saved), and a November cohort with nobody measurable (rate NULL).

Common mistakes. Treating each install as a new user; measuring the window from the latest install; BETWEEN (inclusive end); counting local saves; a plain join to saves before counting; ignoring as_of or excluding only the not-yet-activated unmeasurable users; integer division.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Look back further for a sample of users or use account creation dates; label early cohorts as inflated by returning users rather than silently mixing them. (2) Report a binomial confidence interval (Wilson) or hide rates below a minimum cohort size; trend lines need the interval too. (3) Use the signed-in account, not the device; device-based counting makes every new laptop a new user and inflates acquisition. (4) Keep one row per user and app with first install and first cloud save time; late saves update that row; the cohort report is then a cheap aggregate, recomputed for the cohorts whose windows are still open.

Rubric anchors. 2: computes a rate per cohort but counts reinstalls, uses an inclusive window or counts local saves. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains censoring by as_of, identity choices and how uncertainty would be shown.

Strong signals. Asks what makes a user "new" and whether the window end is inclusive; recognises the censoring problem without prompting. Red flags. Reading document contents to decide activation; device ids as users without comment.

WITH img AS (                          -- exports with a normalised format
  SELECT export_id, app,
         date_trunc('month', exported_ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS month,
         CASE lower(format) WHEN 'jpg' THEN 'jpeg' ELSE lower(format) END AS fmt
  FROM exports
), state AS (                          -- one state per export: its latest non-failed event
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (export_id) export_id, outcome
  FROM manifests
  WHERE outcome <> 'failed'
  ORDER BY export_id, event_ts DESC, manifest_id DESC
), x AS (
  SELECT i.app, i.month, i.fmt, COALESCE(s.outcome = 'embedded', false) AS has_credentials
  FROM img i
  LEFT JOIN state s ON s.export_id = i.export_id
  WHERE i.fmt IN ('jpeg', 'png', 'tiff', 'webp')
)
SELECT app, month, COALESCE(fmt, 'all') AS format,
       COUNT(*)                                  AS image_exports,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE has_credentials)   AS with_credentials,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE has_credentials)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS coverage
FROM x
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((app, month, fmt), (app, month))
HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{min_exports}}
ORDER BY app, month, format;

Explanation. The grain of the report is the export, so the manifest events are reduced to one state per export before the join: the latest event that is not failed (below Very Hard this is simply "has an embedded event"). Formats are normalised once, then filtered to images. GROUPING SETS produces the per-format rows and the 'all' row in one pass; the 'all' row is a real aggregate over every image export of the app and month, not a sum of the rows that survived the floor, and HAVING then applies the floor to every row on its own.

Complexity. A sort for DISTINCT ON over the manifests, a hash join to exports, and a hash aggregate with two grouping sets: O(n log n).

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: GROUPING SETS and COUNTIF; no DISTINCT ON, so QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY export_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC, manifest_id DESC) = 1; DATE_TRUNC(DATE(exported_ts), MONTH). Snowflake: GROUPING SETS, QUALIFY, COUNT_IF. Spark SQL: GROUPING SETS and count_if; row_number in a subquery. MySQL 8: no GROUPING SETS (only WITH ROLLUP, which adds a grand total too), so UNION ALL two aggregates; SUM(CASE …).

Edge cases built into the data. A row exactly at the floor; formats just below it (still in the 'all' row); non-image exports with manifests; exports with no events or only a failed event. Hard: JPG, jpg, Jpeg and other spellings; several events per export (failed then embedded, embedded twice); exports in the last minute of September. Very Hard: an export embedded then stripped (not covered) and one embedded, stripped and embedded again (covered).

Common mistakes. Joining manifests directly (exports counted once per event); counting failed events; lower() without mapping jpg; 'all' computed from the surviving format rows or left out; > for the floor; ignoring stripped; COUNT(DISTINCT export_id) for the total but COUNT(*) of embedded rows for the numerator.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Check whether the export volume or mix changed (a new export path, a new format), whether manifest events are late, and whether the drop is in one app version; only then call it a regression. (2) It is a different metric: "attached at export" versus "still present downstream"; model credential state as events per asset with a separate as-of view. (3) Per-user coverage turns a quality metric into surveillance; answer with per export path, app version and setting, with a minimum group size. (4) Partition by export month, upsert export state from late events, and recompute only the touched app-month-format cells and their 'all' row.

Rubric anchors. 2: plausible coverage but join inflation, unnormalised formats or a wrong 'all' row. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also discusses what coverage does and does not mean, and builds it incrementally.

Strong signals. Says that credentials record provenance and do not prove authenticity; reduces to the export grain before joining; asks whether the floor applies to the 'all' row. Red flags. Proposing to inspect image contents; describing credentials as a guarantee that a file is genuine.

def split_pdf(page_bytes, k, overhead, chapter_starts):
    n = len(page_bytes)
    forced = [False] * n
    forced[0] = True                       # page 1 always starts a part
    for p in chapter_starts:
        forced[p - 1] = True
    if sum(forced) > k:                    # more chapters than parts allowed
        return None

    def parts_needed(cap):                 # greedy: fill each part as far as cap allows
        parts, size = 0, 0
        for b, f in zip(page_bytes, forced):
            if f or size + b > cap:
                parts += 1
                size = overhead + b
            else:
                size += b
        return parts

    lo, hi = overhead + max(page_bytes), overhead + sum(page_bytes)
    while lo < hi:                         # smallest cap that needs at most k parts
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if parts_needed(mid) <= k:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    starts, size = [], 0
    for i, (b, f) in enumerate(zip(page_bytes, forced)):
        if f or size + b > lo:
            starts.append(i + 1)
            size = overhead + b
        else:
            size += b
    return lo, starts

Explanation. The feasibility of a size limit C is monotone: if every part can be kept within C using at most k parts, the same split works for any larger C. So binary-search the smallest feasible C between overhead + max page (no part can be smaller) and overhead + total (one part, which is feasible whenever the chapter count fits). The check fills parts greedily from the front; filling as much as possible never uses more parts than any other split within C (an exchange argument: the greedy part always ends at or after the corresponding part of any other valid split). Chapter starts are forced breaks; the greedy stays optimal with them, and if the chapters alone need more than k parts nothing is feasible. The same greedy at the optimum gives the canonical starts.

Complexity. O(n log S) time for n pages and total size S (about 40 passes of an O(n) loop), O(n) memory. The 60 000-page timing test runs in about 0.2–0.3 s in CPython. A partition DP is O(k·n²): the straightforward version took 3.4 s for only 1 000 pages and k = 40, so 60 000 pages is out of reach.

Dialect notes. Java/C++: use long for sizes (a scanned archive passes 2³¹ bytes easily), and lo + (hi - lo) / 2. Python integers do not overflow. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. k = 1; a single page; k larger than the page count (the largest page decides, small pages still merge); equal pages that divide evenly; one heavy page that must stand alone; a part exactly at the optimum keeps the page. Hard: an overhead large enough that every page is its own part; an overhead with k = 2. Very Hard: a chapter start that forces a split, as many chapters as parts, more chapters than parts (None), chapter_starts containing page 1 and unsorted, a heavy chapter split further inside.

Common mistakes. Starting the search below the largest page plus overhead with a check that does not reject a page larger than the limit (it then accepts sizes no split can meet); size + b >= cap (off by one at the limit); forgetting the overhead for each new part; counting chapter breaks but not the greedy breaks inside chapters; returning the split from the last binary-search probe instead of re-running at the optimum; a DP.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Exchange argument: take an optimal split; move each of its boundaries right until it matches the greedy's; no part exceeds C and the count does not grow. (2) A lexicographic objective (size first, then page-count spread) or a weighted sum; binary search still finds the size, and a second pass balances page counts within it, but a weighted sum needs DP or parametric search. (3) One pass cannot know the optimum; a streaming split with a fixed target (total size known from the file's metadata divided by k, with headroom) is near-optimal and can be corrected at the end. (4) Cap pages per request, compute prefix sums of page sizes at upload, and serve each feasibility check with binary searches on the prefix sums (O(k log n) per check).

Rubric anchors. 2: correct small cases with a DP or a linear search over sizes. 3: all tests pass with binary search and a greedy check. 4: also proves the greedy check and handles chapters and the streaming variant thoughtfully.

Strong signals. States the monotone predicate before coding; picks bounds from the problem; re-runs the greedy for starts. Red flags. Splitting a page; assuming exactly k parts are required.

def sync_plan(local, cloud, base):
    here = dict(local)                     # a later entry for a path replaces an earlier one
    there = dict(cloud)
    synced = dict(base)
    plan = {}
    for path in here.keys() | there.keys() | synced.keys():
        l, c, b = here.get(path), there.get(path), synced.get(path)   # None: absent or deleted
        if l == c:                         # same state on both sides (or both gone)
            plan[path] = 'none'
        elif l == b:                       # only the cloud changed
            plan[path] = 'delete_local' if c is None else 'download'
        elif c == b:                       # only this device changed
            plan[path] = 'delete_cloud' if l is None else 'upload'
        else:                              # both changed, differently
            plan[path] = 'conflict'
    return plan

Explanation. A three-way comparison against the common base, the same idea as a three-way merge. One dictionary per list makes each path's three states O(1) lookups; dict() over a list of pairs keeps the last entry for a path, which is exactly the journal rule, and a None hash or a missing path both read as "does not exist". The four ordered rules then cover every case: agreement, a change on one side only (an edit or a deletion), and a change on both sides.

Complexity. O(n) time and memory for n entries. The 100 000-path timing test runs in about 0.25–0.35 s in CPython. Looking each path up by scanning the three lists took about 2–3 s for only 5 000 paths, so it is hundreds of times too slow at 100 000.

Dialect notes. Java: three HashMap<String, String>s and a HashSet of keys; Objects.equals for null-safe comparison. C++: unordered_map<string, optional<string>>. In SQL this is a FULL OUTER JOIN of three tables on path with the same CASE. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Unchanged; local-only and cloud-only edits; different edits on both sides; the same edit on both sides; new on one side; new on both sides with different contents. Hard: deletion on either side with the other unchanged; deletion against an edit (conflict); deleted on both sides. Very Hard: an edit reverted later in the journal; a None tombstone; deleted then re-created; created and deleted before any sync.

Common mistakes. Comparing local with cloud only (no base), which cannot tell a download from an upload; treating the same edit on both sides as a conflict; forgetting paths that appear only in base; keeping the first journal entry; treating a None hash as a value that differs from "absent"; an O(n²) lookup.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Rules 2 and 3 only fire when one side equals the base, so a change is never overwritten without being the only change; rule 1 hides that both sides changed when they made the same change, which is harmless for contents but loses the fact for audit. (2) A rename looks like a delete plus a new file; a new path whose hash equals a deleted base path's hash is a rename candidate, and an edit on the other side then needs the rename applied first. (3) Derive the copy's name deterministically from the conflicting version (for example its hash or version id and the device), so two devices produce the same name and the second is a no-op. (4) Send a cursor or a per-folder tree of hashes (a Merkle tree) and exchange only changed subtrees.

Rubric anchors. 2: right for edits but wrong for deletions or same-edit cases, or quadratic lookups. 3: all tests pass in O(n). 4: also reasons about renames, conflict copies and incremental sync.

Strong signals. Asks why the base is needed and answers it; checks the both-deleted case; uses a set union of keys. Red flags. "Newest timestamp wins" without discussing clocks; comparing file contents instead of hashes.

def version_diff(old, new, max_edits=None):
    n, m = len(old), len(new)
    # A common start and end need no edits; trimming them is optional but cheap.
    lo = 0
    while lo < n and lo < m and old[lo] == new[lo]:
        lo += 1
    hi_o, hi_n = n, m
    while hi_o > lo and hi_n > lo and old[hi_o - 1] == new[hi_n - 1]:
        hi_o -= 1
        hi_n -= 1
    a, b = old[lo:hi_o], new[lo:hi_n]
    n, m = len(a), len(b)
    limit = n + m if max_edits is None else min(max_edits, n + m)
    off = limit + 1
    v = [0] * (2 * limit + 3)      # v[off + k]: furthest x reached on diagonal k = x - y
    for d in range(limit + 1):
        for k in range(-d, d + 1, 2):
            if k == -d or (k != d and v[off + k - 1] < v[off + k + 1]):
                x = v[off + k + 1]          # step down: insert b[y]
            else:
                x = v[off + k - 1] + 1      # step right: delete a[x]
            y = x - k
            while x < n and y < m and a[x] == b[y]:
                x += 1                      # follow the snake of equal paragraphs
                y += 1
            v[off + k] = x
            if x >= n and y >= m:
                return ((d + n - m) // 2, (d - n + m) // 2)
    return None

Explanation. This is Myers' greedy algorithm (1986) for the shortest edit script with insertions and deletions only. In the edit graph, x indexes old and y indexes new. A right step deletes, a down step inserts, and a diagonal step over equal paragraphs is free. For each number of edits d, v[k] holds the furthest x that any path with d edits reaches on diagonal k = x − y. Keeping only the furthest point is safe: from a point further along the same diagonal you can do everything a nearer point can, since the remaining sub-problem is a suffix of it. A d-edit path ends on a diagonal from −d to d with the parity of d. Each round extends every diagonal by one edit from its better neighbour, then follows free diagonal steps (the "snake") as far as they go. The first d whose path reaches (n, m) is the minimum D, and deleted = (D + n − m) / 2, inserted = (D − n + m) / 2, which equal n − LCS and m − LCS. With a cap, the loop simply stops after max_edits rounds and returns None. Trimming the common start and end is a standard speed-up and does not change the answer.

Complexity. O((n + m) · D) time in the worst case and O(n + m) memory (only the current v). On the timing test (30 000 paragraphs, about 80 edit sites spread through the document, so D ≈ 100 to 110) it does O(n + D²) work in practice because the hashes are mostly distinct, and it runs in about 0.01 s in CPython. The full LCS table is 9 × 10⁸ cells: extrapolated from measured runs at 1 500 and 3 000 paragraphs, about 110 s in CPython, and the table alone would not fit in memory if kept whole. A banded DP that only fills cells within D of the diagonal is also O((n + m) · D) but always fills the whole band; at this size it is several seconds in CPython and may miss the limit. Accept it in discussion as a correct output-sensitive idea. Hunt–Szymanski, which is fast when few pairs of paragraphs match, also passes here and is acceptable with a stated complexity.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++ the same loop uses an int[] of size 2·limit + 3; the GNU diff and git default diff are Myers variants with heuristics that may give up minimality on huge inputs. difflib.SequenceMatcher in Python is not a minimal edit-distance algorithm. In SQL, a minimal diff is impractical; a warehouse would compare versions by joining on paragraph id, which only works if paragraphs have stable ids. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Identical versions; both empty; old empty; new empty; one rewritten paragraph; one moved paragraph; swapped neighbours; a reversed order; a common run that is not at the start; (Hard) repeated empty-paragraph hashes that must align correctly and a whole section moved; (Very Hard) exactly max_edits, one over the cap, a cap of 0 on identical and on different versions, and a cap larger than both versions.

Common mistakes. Counting a rewritten paragraph as one edit (that is Levenshtein with substitutions, a different metric); returning None when the edits equal the cap; using difflib and assuming minimality; positional comparison (old[i] != new[i]), which counts every paragraph after an insertion as changed; building the n × m table; assuming hashes are unique when the replay says they repeat; off-by-one in the diagonal offset when max_edits is 0.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Store v for every round (O(D²) memory, fine for small D) and backtrack, or use Myers' linear-space divide-and-conquer that finds the middle snake and recurses. (2) After the diff, match deleted and inserted paragraphs by hash: equal hashes in the two lists are moves; show them as moved with a link. Patience or histogram diff, which anchor on unique lines, also give more readable results. (3) Run a word-level diff within paired changed paragraphs, and fall back to "rewritten" when the word-level D exceeds a fraction of the length, using the same cap idea. (4) A three-way merge diffs each side against the common base; non-overlapping changes apply automatically, and overlapping ones go to the author as a conflict.

Rubric anchors. 2: a correct but O(n · m) DP, or positional comparison; the timing test fails. 3: Myers or another output-sensitive algorithm, all tests pass, complexity stated. 4: also explains why the furthest point per diagonal suffices, handles the cap cleanly as an early exit, and gives credible answers on recovering the script in linear space and on moves.

Strong signals. Asks whether moves count as one edit; estimates the n × m table before coding; notes that trimming the common start and end does not help when edits are spread out. Red flags. Insisting difflib is minimal; counting substitutions; ignoring memory.

ADB-L2-02.html:
Reference solution

def break_lines(widths, line_width, space, forced):
    n = len(widths)
    for w in widths:
        if w > line_width:
            return None
    hard = set(forced)
    best = [0] * (n + 1)        # best[i]: least cost to lay out words i..n-1
    nxt = [n] * (n + 1)         # start of the line after the one that starts at i
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        length = -space
        bc = -1
        bj = n
        j = i
        while j < n:
            length += space + widths[j]
            if length > line_width:
                break                           # no longer line can fit either
            if j == n - 1 or j in hard:
                c = best[j + 1]                 # a last line, or one ended by a forced break, is free
            else:
                s = line_width - length
                c = s * s + best[j + 1]
            if bc < 0 or c < bc:                # strict: on a tie keep the earlier break
                bc, bj = c, j + 1
            if j in hard:
                break                           # no line runs past a forced break
            j += 1
        best[i], nxt[i] = bc, bj
    starts = []
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        starts.append(i)
        i = nxt[i]
    return (best[0], starts)

Explanation. best[i] is the least cost of laying out words i to the end. The line starting at i ends at some j; its cost is the squared slack, or 0 if it is the last line (or, at Very Hard, ends at a forced break), plus best[j + 1]. Because widths and spaces are positive, the line's width only grows with j, so once it no longer fits the loop stops: that bounds the inner loop by the number of words that fit on a line. Filling from the end and keeping the earliest j on a strict tie gives the lexicographically smallest starts list: every candidate from i begins with i, then the next start j decides the comparison, and among equal j the rest is best[j + 1]'s own smallest list. (A proper prefix never ties: if the remaining words fit on one free line, any extra break adds a line with positive slack.) A word wider than the line makes every layout illegal, so the answer is None. Iteration rather than recursion avoids Python's recursion limit on 80 000 words.

Complexity. O(n · w) time, where w is the most words on a line, and O(n) memory. The timing test (80 000 words of 2 to 12 units, a 72-unit line, about 9 words a line) runs in about 0.25 s in CPython. Trying every later word as a line end, even with prefix sums for the widths, is O(n²): measured at about 1 s for 4 000 words and 4.2 s for 8 000, so about 7 minutes at 80 000.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++ the same loop uses long costs (a 1 000-unit line squared is 10⁶ per line, and a long paragraph adds many lines). TeX's Knuth–Plass algorithm uses the same DP idea over feasible breakpoints, with badness, penalties and demerits instead of squared slack. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. An empty paragraph; everything on one free line; a word exactly as wide as the line; a line that fills exactly; a paragraph where first-fit is not optimal; one where the free last line changes the layout; (Hard) wider spaces, a tie broken by the smaller starts list, every word on its own line; (Very Hard) a word wider than the line (None), a forced break after the first word, a forced break after the last word, and two forced breaks.

Common mistakes. Greedy first-fit; charging the last line; counting a space after the last word of a line; an inner loop that continues instead of breaks when the line is too long (correct, quadratic); recursion that hits the recursion limit; returning the break after each line (j) instead of the start of each line; a tie rule implemented with <=, which keeps the later break; letting a line run past a forced break.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Carry the previous line's tightness class in the state (a few classes, as Knuth–Plass does), multiplying states by a small constant. (2) Recompute from the paragraph that changed; a layout from that paragraph onward stops changing once a line break coincides with the old layout at a point where the downstream state is the same, so relayout can stop there (paragraph-level independence makes this easy unless pages and columns interact). (3) Hyphenation points become extra candidate break positions inside words, with a fixed penalty added to the line cost. (4) The cost of a line as a function of its start and end has the Monge (quadrangle) property for convex functions of slack, which SMAWK or the Hirschberg–Larmore approach exploits for O(n) or O(n log n); squared slack is convex, but the infeasible-width cutoff needs care.

Rubric anchors. 2: greedy, or a correct DP that is O(n²) or recursive and fails the large test. 3: correct DP with the bounded inner loop, the tie rule and the special cases; all tests pass. 4: also proves the tie rule and the early break, avoids recursion deliberately, and gives a credible answer on incremental relayout or richer costs.

Strong signals. Asks whether the last line counts and how spaces are measured before coding; writes the counterexample to greedy unprompted. Red flags. "Greedy is how word processors do it" with no cost argument; floats for an integer cost.

ADB-L2-03.html:
Reference solution (the fixed report)

from datetime import datetime, timezone


def _month(ts):
    # The month is the UTC calendar month of the event, not the local date in the string.
    return datetime.fromisoformat(ts).astimezone(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m")


def font_usage_report(events):
    report = {}
    for ev in events:
        if ev["type"] != "activate":
            continue                                   # deactivations are never counted
        family, style = ev["font"].split("/", 1)
        style = style.split("@", 1)[0]                 # a variable-font instance is its style
        row = report.setdefault(_month(ev["ts"]), {}).setdefault(family, {
            "desktop_activations": 0,
            "desktop_accounts": set(),
            "styles": set(),
            "web_projects": set(),
        })
        if ev["surface"] == "web":
            row["web_projects"].add(ev["project"])
        else:
            row["desktop_activations"] += 1            # desktop only
            row["desktop_accounts"].add(ev["account"])  # per family, not per style
        row["styles"].add(style)
    return {
        month: {
            family: {
                "desktop_activations": row["desktop_activations"],
                "desktop_accounts": len(row["desktop_accounts"]),
                "styles": len(row["styles"]),
                "web_projects": len(row["web_projects"]),
            }
            for family, row in families.items()
        }
        for month, families in report.items()
    }

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Month from the local string. ts[:7] takes the local date. Symptom: activations on the last evening of a month in the Americas, and the first morning of a month east of UTC, land in the wrong month. Fix: parse with the offset and convert to UTC before taking the month.
  2. Variable-font instances kept as styles. The style keeps @wght=…,wdth=…, so each instance is a new style. Symptom: families with variable fonts appear to have hundreds of styles. Fix: take the part before @.
  3. Accounts counted per style. The account set holds (account, style). Symptom: an account that activated Regular and Bold counts twice, so desktop accounts exceed real users. Fix: add the account alone.
  4. Web additions counted as desktop activity. Desktop counters are updated for every event. Symptom: desktop activations and accounts jump in months with big web launches. Fix: update them only for desktop events.
  5. Deactivations counted. Nothing checks type. Symptom: switching a font off counts as using it, adds a web project when it is removed from one, and creates rows for families nobody activated. Fix: skip non-activate events at the top, before the row is created.

Each bug has its own check that fails on it alone: an evening in UTC−05:00 and a morning in UTC+05:30 at month ends (bug 1), two accounts on two instances of one variable style (bug 2), one account with two styles (bug 3), a desktop activation plus a web addition (bug 4), and an activation followed by a deactivation, plus a family that was only deactivated (bug 5). Bugs 2 and 3 interact: with bug 2 still present, one account activating two instances of one variable style is counted as two accounts by bug 3. Fixing bug 3 alone fixes that case; worth asking the candidate to explain.

Explanation. A usage report is a set of counters, each with a grain (per month and family), a filter (which event types and surfaces) and a distinctness key (accounts, styles or projects). Every bug here gets one of those three wrong, plus the time-zone rule that decides the month.

Complexity. O(n) time and O(distinct keys) memory. The timing test is 200 000 events and runs in about 0.8 s in CPython, mostly in timestamp parsing; caching the month per timestamp string helps when timestamps repeat.

Dialect notes. In SQL: date_trunc('month', ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') in PostgreSQL, DATE_TRUNC('MONTH', CONVERT_TIMEZONE('UTC', ts)) in Snowflake, DATE_TRUNC(DATE(ts, 'UTC'), MONTH) in BigQuery; the distinct counts become COUNT(DISTINCT account) FILTER (WHERE surface = 'desktop') in PostgreSQL and COUNT(DISTINCT IF(surface = 'desktop', account, NULL)) in BigQuery; split_part(style, '@', 1) reduces instances. Taking substr(ts_string, 1, 7) reproduces bug 1. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Month-end evening west of UTC; month-start morning east of UTC; two instances of one variable style; one account with two styles; a desktop activation and a web addition; an activation then a deactivation; a family only deactivated; the same style activated twice by one account; two families.

Common mistakes. Fixing the month with a fixed offset or the server's local zone; stripping @… only for desktop events; filtering deactivations after the row is created, which still leaves empty rows; fixing the desktop counters but also dropping web events from styles; rewriting the function instead of making minimal fixes.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Activity at any point in the month needs state: each (account, font) active interval from activations and deactivations, carried across months from the previous month's open intervals; then count accounts whose interval overlaps the month. (2) Partition by event date, re-run the affected months idempotently (overwrite the month's rows), and accept events up to the lateness window; after that, either restate with a log or report them in the next run with a note. (3) Approximate distinct counts (HyperLogLog) are fine for dashboards and trends; payments to type designers, if they depend on usage, need exact counts or a documented approximation agreed with them. (4) Key families by a stable id, keep a name history with validity dates, and report by id with the name as of the report date; old reports show the name they used.

Rubric anchors. 2: finds two or three bugs, some checks still fail. 3: all five fixed, all checks pass, each explained with its symptom. 4: also states each counter's grain, filter and key, adds a test per bug, notices the interaction between bugs 2 and 3, and answers the active-state and late-event follow-ups concretely.

Strong signals. Tries a month-end timestamp in a negative offset first; asks what a "style" is for a variable font. Red flags. "Use the local month, the user sees local time" without noticing the report is defined in UTC; deleting deactivation events from storage.

ADB-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Upload and landing. Contributors upload through resumable uploads into object storage under an upload id. The service records (upload_id, contributor_id, content_hash, size, media_type, uploaded_at). An exact duplicate (same contributor, same content hash) returns the existing asset instead of creating another. Near-duplicates across contributors are detected later by a perceptual-hash check, not at upload.
  • Asset and state machine. assets (asset_id, contributor_id, content_hash, media_type, current_state, current_metadata_version) plus an append-only asset_events (asset_id, seq, from_state, to_state, actor, reason_code, metadata_version, at). States: uploaded → checks_passed | checks_failed → submitted → in_review → approved | rejected; approved → withdrawn (by the contributor) | taken_down (by the marketplace). Transitions are validated against the allowed graph, and the state column is derived from the events in the same transaction.
  • Checks. Automated checks (format, resolution, corruption, duplicate) write check_results (asset_id, check, version, outcome, details, at). Technical failures may reject automatically with a reason code; everything else proceeds to human review.
  • Metadata. asset_metadata (asset_id, version, title, keywords[], categories, licence_type, edited_by, edited_at) is versioned; review decisions reference the metadata version they saw. Releases for people or property are stored as documents with their own ids, linked to the asset; analytics read only their status and dates, never their contents.
  • Review queues. Queues by media type and language, ordered by submission age. Each assignment and decision is an event. Decision time is measured per asset from submitted to decision, against {{review_target}}.
  • Search freshness. Changes leave the database through a transactional outbox (or CDC) into a log keyed by asset_id, so updates for one asset stay in order. An indexer applies them to the search index with the asset's event sequence as the document version, and the index rejects writes older than the version it has. Takedowns and withdrawals are written to the same key and also to a small high-priority topic, so they are applied within {{freshness}} even when the main topic lags; because of versioning, a stale keyword edit can never re-add a taken-down asset. Licensing checks the asset table, not the index, so a takedown stops new licences immediately.
  • Rebuild. The index is a projection: a full rebuild reads the asset table at a recorded log position, builds a new index, replays the log from that position, and switches an alias atomically.
  • Metrics. Queue size and age per queue; decisions per hour; share of decisions within {{review_target}}; rejection reasons per category; index lag (event time to searchable) at percentiles, with a separate measure for takedowns; index-to-table disagreement counts from a daily reconciliation.

Competing designs to accept. A workflow engine that owns the state machine (accept if transitions and reasons are still recorded as data); a search index updated synchronously from the API (accept for low volume if failures are retried and reconciled); a periodic full reindex plus a fast delta path. Accept any design that keeps the index rebuildable and guarantees takedown ordering.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A current-state column with no history, so rejections cannot be explained; out-of-order updates resurrecting a taken-down asset in search; a reindex that serves a half-built index; review queues dominated by one large contributor's batch; duplicate assets from retried uploads; release documents leaking into analytics.

Incident guidance. Not required for Loop 2; use the follow-ups. If the candidate raises incidents, look for: index lag alerts separate for takedowns, reconciliation between the index and the asset table, and a replayable log.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Both updates go through the same key with versions; the takedown has a higher version, so the keyword edit, if applied later, is rejected by the version check; the high-priority path only makes it faster. (2) Queue age and arrivals per queue, reviewer throughput, rejection mix; then rebalance queues, cap per-contributor daily submissions, add automated checks for the commonest rejection reasons. (3) Build a new index from a snapshot plus log replay, verify counts and samples, and switch the alias; the old index keeps serving until then. (4) Perceptual hashes with a similarity threshold, a candidate list for reviewers, and a policy decision (for example, the earlier approved asset keeps priority); the second contributor sees a reason code.

Rubric anchors. 2: an asset table with a status column and a nightly reindex; no history; takedowns not guaranteed. 3: append-only state transitions with reasons, versioned metadata, an ordered change log into a rebuildable index, and takedowns that cannot be overtaken. 4: also duplicate handling at upload and across contributors, licensing that does not depend on the index, review metrics against the target, and a zero-downtime rebuild.

Strong signals. Asks whether a takedown must also stop new licences; uses the event sequence as the index version. Red flags. "The search index is the source of truth"; deleting rejected assets with no record.

ADB-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Collection endpoint. Stateless edge collectors accept hits over HTTPS (and batched POSTs from apps), validate the tag id against the customer registry, check consent flags (a hit the visitor did not consent to is dropped before storage, and only a count of dropped hits is kept), stamp server receive time, derive device and coarse geography from the request, then discard or truncate the IP address. They write to the buffer and only then return success.
  • Hit identity. (tag_id, visitor_id, visit_id, seq) from the tag, or a client-generated hit id. Retries carry the same identity. Deduplication happens downstream in the stream processor with a keyed state store whose TTL covers the retry horizon plus the late window for app batches, and again when finished days are built.
  • Buffer. A partitioned log keyed by (customer, visitor_id), so a visitor's hits stay in order and a customer spreads across partitions. Per-customer quotas and an overflow path protect others during a campaign; very large customers have dedicated partitions.
  • Processing. Apply the customer's processing rules in effect at processing time, record which rule version was applied, map events to the customer's definitions, and sessionise per visitor: a visit ends after 30 minutes without a hit or at the end of the day in the customer's report time zone (this exercise's rule). Device time is used for ordering within a visit; if it disagrees with server time by more than a threshold, server time wins and the hit is flagged.
  • Bot filtering. Known bot user agents and lists you are given, plus behaviour rules (implausible rates, no rendering events, monitoring patterns). Filtered hits go to a separate table with the rule id and version, never deleted, so customers can see what was removed and a rule can be reversed.
  • Layers. Raw hits as received (immutable, partitioned by customer and receive date) → a real-time layer updated within {{report_latency}}, approximate and labelled as such → finished days built after the late window of {{late_window}} closes, from raw hits by a deterministic job that overwrites the day's partition. Later arrivals are stored in raw and listed in a late-hits table; adding them to a finished day is an explicit, logged re-run, not a silent change.
  • Isolation. Customer id is in every key, path and query predicate; reports are served through a service that enforces it.
  • Completeness metrics. Hits received, accepted, dropped (with reason: invalid tag, no consent, malformed), deduplicated, filtered as bots, processed; per customer and hour; lag per partition; late-hit volume by age. Optional: the tag sends a sequence number per visit, so gaps estimate hits lost between the browser and the collector.

Competing designs to accept. A lambda-style design (stream for real-time, batch for finished days) or a kappa design (one stream job with replay for re-runs); a lakehouse table format with MERGE for late hits; sessionisation done in batch only (accept if real-time numbers are clearly labelled as visit-free counts). Accept designs that keep raw immutable and finished days reproducible.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Hot partitions from one customer's campaign; a deduplication store too small for the app late window; storing hits before checking consent; IP addresses persisted; visits split by late hits; bot rules applied silently and irreversibly; finished days that keep changing; device clocks set years off.

Incident guidance. Not required for Loop 2; use the follow-ups. If the candidate raises incidents, look for per-customer lag alerts, a dropped-hit breakdown, and a re-run log for finished days.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Quotas and overflow at the edge, partitions keyed so the customer spreads; their lag rises, others' does not; real-time numbers for that customer are delayed and labelled. (2) Stored in raw and listed as late; finished days unchanged until an explicit re-run, which the customer sees in a change log with counts; real-time views never double count them. (3) Run the rule in shadow mode, compare filtered volumes and sample hits, review with the customer, then enable from a date with a note; never restate silently. (4) Per-customer completeness: received versus processed with reasons for every difference, and sequence gaps per visit as an estimate of loss before collection.

Rubric anchors. 2: a collector writing straight to a warehouse table; no hit identity; bots deleted; late hits appended to finished days. 3: durable buffer before acknowledgement, deduplication on hit identity, per-customer isolation, clear visit rule, bots recorded separately, raw / real-time / finished layers. 4: also consent before storage and IP handling, hot-customer handling, explicit late-hit and re-run policy, and completeness metrics a customer can audit.

Strong signals. Asks how long app batches can be delayed before choosing a deduplication window; separates "received" from "counted" in metrics. Red flags. Storing full IP addresses "for later"; filtering bots by deleting hits.

ADB-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Documents. documents (document_id, owner_id, owner_org_id NULL, created_at, created_by_app, deleted_at NULL, purged_at NULL). Ownership transfers are rows in document_ownership (document_id, owner_id, owner_org_id, valid_from, valid_to), so "outside the organisation" can be computed as of any date.
  • Versions. document_versions (version_id, document_id, seq, kind autosave|manual|restore, based_on_version_id, restored_from_version_id NULL, committed_at (server), client_saved_at, app, app_version, device_class, size_bytes, component_count, content_ref, contents_deleted_at NULL). Append-only; seq is assigned by the service per document, so ordering never depends on device clocks. content_ref points to stored contents; retention clears the contents and sets contents_deleted_at, but the row stays as a tombstone.
  • Names. version_names (version_id, name, named_by, named_at, removed_at NULL): a history, so a rename is a new row. A version with an active name is exempt from retention; removing the last name makes it eligible again from that moment.
  • Current version. Derived: the version with the highest seq committed at or before t. A cached current_version_id on the document is acceptable for serving if it is verified against the derivation; it is never the source for history.
  • Sharing. access_grants (grant_id, document_id, principal_type person|link|org, principal_id, role viewer|commenter|editor, granted_by, valid_from, valid_to NULL, change_reason). A role change closes the open row and opens a new one; revocation closes it; a link toggled off and on is two intervals. "Who could edit at t" = owner as of t ∪ grants with role editor and valid_from ≤ t < valid_to.
  • Comments. comments (comment_id, document_id, version_id, anchor (region or object id + coordinates), author_id, created_at, resolved_at NULL, resolved_by) and comment_replies. The anchor keeps the original version; carry-forward to later versions is computed by the app (object still exists) and may be cached in comment_anchor_resolution (comment_id, version_id, status shown|orphaned).
  • Analytics facts (no contents). fct_version_saved (one row per version: document, app, kind, size, committed date), fct_document_day (document × day: versions saved, active editors, apps), fct_sharing_interval derived from grants, fct_comment (created, resolved, time to resolution, anchor status). File names, layer names and text never leave the operational store.
  • Estimate. At follow-up 3's numbers: 3% of {{documents}} documents edited for two hours with a version every {{autosave_minutes}} minutes is the version-row count per day; tens to hundreds of millions of small rows a day at the top level, which is fine as an append-only partitioned table, while daily aggregates serve most dashboards.

Competing designs to accept. A single event log of document actions (saved, named, restored, shared, commented) with projections for versions, grants and comments, as long as as-of queries are defined on it. Type 2 history on the grant table instead of explicit intervals (equivalent). Storing named-ness as an attribute of the version row with a separate audit table for renames.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. An is_current flag flipped in place (no history, races between devices); grants overwritten or deleted (access history lost); deleting version rows under retention (comments, names and restore lineage dangle); ordering versions by device time; counting autosaves as user activity without separating kinds; contents (file or layer names) leaking into analytics.

Incident guidance.

  • Retention deleted metadata rows: the job removed the row, not just the contents. Stop the job; restore the rows from the backup or the change log (contents are gone, metadata is not); make retention clear content_ref and set contents_deleted_at only; add a foreign-key or integrity check that every comment, name and based_on_version_id resolves before the job commits. Retention period ({{unnamed_retention_days}} days) unchanged.
  • Autosave every few seconds: detect from versions per document-hour against the expected rate (one per {{autosave_minutes}} minutes while editing); contain by rate-limiting accepted autosaves server-side or coalescing them; report the metric by kind and exclude the affected app version from comparisons, with an annotation; add an alert on versions per active document by app version.
  • Grants updated in place: rebuild the history from the sharing audit log or change capture if it exists, and say plainly what cannot be reconstructed; move to effective-dated grants with closes instead of updates and deletes; add a test that a revocation leaves a closed interval.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Max seq with committed_at ≤ t; grants with valid_from ≤ t < coalesce(valid_to, ∞) plus the owner as of t, link principals included. (2) The comment still points at the tombstoned version; the panel shows it as "on a removed version" with its anchor resolved against the nearest later version if possible. (3) Version rows at version grain for recent months, document-day aggregates for history. (4) A new ownership interval; grants stay; past months are not restated because ownership is as-of. (5) The model proves which grants existed and which link was on; it cannot prove who received a forwarded link, only who opened it if access logs exist.

Rubric anchors. 2: a documents table with a current version column and a permissions table updated in place. 3: immutable versions with lineage, derived current version, effective-dated grants, comments on versions, tombstones under retention. 4: also names as history, link principals, ownership as of a date, carry-forward rules for comments, an estimate and content-free facts.

Strong signals. Asks "as of when?" before drawing tables; separates version metadata from stored contents. Red flags. Deleting rows to apply retention; ordering by device clock; file or layer names in analytics.

ADB-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Agreements. agreements (agreement_id, account_id, sender_id, template_id NULL, template_version NULL, created_at, sent_at NULL, expires_at NULL, signing_mode sequential|parallel|groups). No mutable status as source of truth; the lifecycle is derived from events (a cached status is fine for serving).
  • Documents. agreement_documents (agreement_id, document_ref, page_count, size_bytes, position): references and metadata only.
  • Plan (frozen at send). participant_sets (agreement_id, set_id, order_no); participant_slots (agreement_id, slot_id, set_id, role signer|approver|form_filler|cc, original_participant_id). Edits before sending create a new plan version; after sending the plan is immutable (a sender's "replace participant" is an event, not an edit).
  • Events (append-only). agreement_events (event_id, agreement_id, slot_id NULL, actor_participant_id, type created|sent|viewed|reminder_sent|delegated|signed|approved|declined|cancelled|expired|completed, delegate_to NULL, occurred_at, recorded_at, seq). seq per agreement gives the true order even with equal timestamps. Delegation: an event on the slot from the current holder to delegate_to; the holder at time t is the end of the chain of delegations at or before t.
  • Audit trail versus analytics. The audit trail store keeps the full record the customer downloads (including identities and what the service records as evidence), hash-chained per agreement for tamper evidence, retained {{audit_retention_years}} years. Analytics receives an allowlisted projection: ids pseudonymised per customer, event types, roles, timestamps, page counts; never field values, document contents, signature images or email addresses. The projection is defined by a schema registry where every field is classified, and unknown fields are dropped, not passed.
  • Facts. fct_agreement (accumulating snapshot: sent, completed/declined/cancelled/expired at, outcome, template and template version, participant and set counts, total wait); fct_slot (one row per slot: set order, role, became_actionable_at, acted_at, delegation hops, reminders received, outcome); fct_agreement_event (event grain, short retention). Stall = the set an open agreement is waiting on, measured from when it became actionable.
  • As-of reconstruction. Read the frozen plan, then events with occurred_at ≤ t ordered by seq: completed sets advance the order, delegations move holders, declines and cancellations end it.

Competing designs to accept. Event sourcing with the agreement aggregate as a projection; a slot-state table updated by the service plus the event log as history (if as-of comes from events). Pseudonymising participants with a keyed hash per customer, or with a mapping table in the operational store.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Wide rows with signer1..signerN columns; status overwritten so past state is lost; delegation stored by replacing the participant (original lost); analytics fed raw events (field values and emails leak); template joined at current version; reminders counted from the scheduler rather than from sent events; one analytics retention for audit purposes.

Incident guidance.

  • Field values in the event payload: a contents leak. Stop the projection for that event type, purge the field from every analytics table, staging area and backup in scope, and record what was exposed for the customers affected (their notification follows the company's process). Guardrail: allowlisted projection from a classified schema; new fields blocked until classified; a scanner that fails the pipeline on unexpected payload keys.
  • Double reminders after failover: deduplicate reminder events by (agreement, slot, scheduled window) and correct the metric; make the scheduler idempotent with a per-slot reminder key every {{reminder_days}} days; tell affected customers what happened.
  • Reports joined to current template: pin template_version on the agreement at send; rebuild last quarter's stall report from the pinned version and publish it as a correction.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Plan plus events up to t in seq order; current set = lowest set with an incomplete slot. (2) Stall measured from when the set became actionable; delegations and reminders shown as counts on the slot. (3) Each agreement keeps the version it was sent with. (4) The audit store answers, with its hash chain and sequence numbers as proof of completeness and order; analytics never does. (5) Slot grain for the facts that need it (stalls, delegation), agreement grain for completion times; events at full grain only briefly.

Rubric anchors. 2: one agreements table with status and participant columns, analytics on raw events. 3: frozen plan with sets and slots, append-only events, delegation lineage, derived lifecycle, content-free projection, facts at stated grains. 4: also a classified allowlist, audit retention apart from analytics, as-of reconstruction, template versions pinned and incident handling with purge and guardrail.

Strong signals. Draws the audit/analytics boundary unprompted; keeps the original participant on delegation. Red flags. Field values or emails in analytics; deleting or overwriting events; treating the analytics warehouse as the customer's audit record.

ADB-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Manifests. manifests (manifest_id, asset_hash, hash_alg, claim_generator_app, app_version, signer_cert_id, signed_at, identity_included bool, standard_version, created_by_feature). Immutable. An edit produces a new manifest that lists the previous asset as an ingredient.
  • Actions. manifest_actions (manifest_id, ordinal, action_kind crop|resize|color_adjust|generative_fill|generative_expand|…, generative bool, feature, model_family NULL). No prompts, no parameters that carry user text.
  • Ingredients. manifest_ingredients (manifest_id, ordinal, ingredient_asset_hash, ingredient_manifest_id NULL, relationship parentOf|componentOf|inputTo). A DAG keyed by hash; the same ingredient can appear many times.
  • Storage. manifest_locations (manifest_id, location embedded|cloud, stored_at, removed_at NULL).
  • Signers and trust. signer_certs (cert_id, issuer, valid_from, valid_to); trust_lists (trust_list_version, effective_from) and trust_list_entries (trust_list_version, cert_id).
  • Verifications. verifications (verification_id, inspected_hash, checked_at, trust_list_version, outcome valid|signature_invalid|untrusted_signer|asset_modified|no_credentials|recovered_from_cloud, manifest_id NULL, source upload|url). Append-only, reproducible from (hash, manifest, trust list version). The inspected file is hashed and discarded.
  • Lineage. Bounded recursive CTE over manifest_ingredients for ad hoc questions; for hot queries a closure table manifest_ancestry (descendant_manifest_id, ancestor_asset_hash, depth) maintained incrementally: a new manifest inherits its ingredients' ancestry plus the ingredients themselves (insert-only, because manifests never change). Fan-out from a hugely shared ingredient is served by the descendant index on ancestor_asset_hash with pagination, never by an unbounded walk.
  • Facts. fct_export_credential (export grain: app, month, generative bool, ingredient count, identity flag); fct_verification_week (outcome × week × source). Report wording: "valid means the manifest is intact, bound to this file and signed by a recognised signer; it does not establish that the content is true".

Competing designs to accept. Storing the manifest as a JSON document plus extracted columns (actions and ingredients as rows or arrays) for analytics. A graph database for lineage, if the analytics tables still exist. Computing ancestry on read with depth limits instead of a closure table, if they show the cost bound.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A mutable is_valid flag; recomputing past outcomes against today's trust list; "valid" described as authenticity; unbounded recursion from a popular ingredient; closure table rebuilt nightly instead of incrementally; prompts or uploaded files retained; identity stored in analytics; "no credentials" on re-shared copies conflated with exports that lacked credentials.

Incident guidance.

  • Trust list removal rewrote history: past outcomes are observations with their trust list version and must not be recomputed. Restore the stored results, show the dashboard by trust list version (with a marker on the change date), and add a test that the results table is insert-only.
  • Site strips metadata: a re-shared copy without an embedded manifest is not an export without credentials. Split the weekly report by source and by "recovered from cloud"; compute export coverage (about {{generative_share}} of exports with a generative step) from export facts, not from inspections.
  • Closure job ran nine hours: the nightly full rebuild met an ingredient used {{max_ingredients}} times per composite and re-exported thousands of times. Switch to incremental insert-only ancestry per new manifest, deduplicate repeated ingredients per manifest, and serve fan-out queries from the descendant index with limits.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Recursive CTE from X's hash through manifest_ingredients to descendants, with a depth limit and a visited set; for huge fan-out, the closure table and pagination. (2) Yesterday's results stay; new checks get the new outcome; the weekly share is shown by trust list version. (3) An outcome "recovered from cloud", distinct from "found embedded" and "no credentials". (4) Edges per day ≈ exports × average ingredients; insert-only closure rows grow with depth, so cap depth or store ancestry only to a fixed depth plus a pointer. (5) Past manifests are immutable; analytics only has the flag, and future exports carry the flag set to false.

Rubric anchors. 2: one assets table with an authenticity flag. 3: immutable manifests, actions and ingredients as rows, verification as observations with trust list version, no prompts. 4: also a lineage strategy with cost bounds, precise outcome categories including recovery, wording that rules out an authenticity claim, and the incidents handled.

Strong signals. Separates "what the manifest says" from "what a check found"; bounds the graph walk unprompted. Red flags. "Verified = authentic"; storing prompts or inspected files; updating outcomes in place.

ADB-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Libraries. libraries (library_id, owner_id, org_id NULL, created_at); library_members (library_id, member_id, role viewer|editor, valid_from, valid_to NULL).
  • Elements. elements (element_id, library_id, kind color|char_style|para_style|graphic|logo, created_at, deleted_at NULL, copied_from_element_id NULL); element_versions (element_id, version_no, published_at, published_by, change_kind edit|rename|revert|restore|delete, value_ref). version_no is assigned by the library service under a per-element lock or compare-and-set, never by the client.
  • Placements. placements (document_id, document_version_id, placement_id, element_id, applied_version_no, mode linked|embedded, unlinked_at NULL), recorded from each saved document version's metadata. The latest document version gives the current state.
  • Reverse index. element_links (element_id, document_id, latest_document_version_id, applied_version_no, mode, observed_at) derived from placements, upserted by document version order (a late offline version older than the stored one never overwrites it).
  • Propagation events. propagation_events (element_id, version_no, document_id, event published|notified|applied, occurred_at). Apply only if version_no > applied_version_no: monotonic, so out-of-order updates can't go backwards.
  • Staleness. A linked placement is out of date when applied_version_no < the element's latest version. Categories: pending (document not opened since publish), blocked (owner has no access to the library as of now), kept (unlinked on purpose, excluded from out of date), failed (opened but not applied: a defect).
  • Facts. fct_element_reach (element, day: linked documents, out-of-date by category); fct_propagation (element version × document: published_at, applied_at, open_at_publish bool). Latency for open documents uses published → applied with the {{propagation_minutes}}-minute target; closed documents are reported as "time to first open after publish", separately, so both populations are visible.
  • Access. Brand teams see document owners only for documents shared with them; other documents as counts.

Competing designs to accept. An event-sourced placement log with the reverse index as a projection. Storing placements only for the latest document version plus a change log (if history can be rebuilt). Push propagation versus pull on open, if the measurement covers both.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. An array of documents on the element row (hot row, unbounded growth); last-write-wins on updates (reverts lost, versions go backwards); client-assigned version numbers; reverse index ignoring late offline saves; latency measured only on open documents; unlinked or blocked placements counted as out of date forever; deleting placements when an element is deleted.

Incident guidance.

  • Edit and revert applied in different orders: documents compared timestamps or applied in arrival order. Enforce applying only higher version_no; re-publish the latest version to every linked document (the revert is version n+2, so it wins); add an invariant check that applied_version_no never decreases per placement.
  • Library unshared from an agency: those placements are blocked, not pending. Classify them as blocked from the membership interval, exclude them from the actionable count (still show them), and give the brand team a list of affected documents shared with them; alert when a category grows without any open events.
  • Latency only on open documents: the percentile hid the closed-document population. Report two measures (open: publish → applied; closed: publish → first open → applied) and a share of documents updated within the target, and annotate the change.

Follow-up guidance. (1) From the reverse index for the element: linked placements with applied < latest, split by category; one indexed read per element, proportional to the linked documents. (2) Open document: applies n+1 then n+2 (or only n+2 if both arrive together); closed: applies n+2 on open. (3) published_at to applied_at on the document's device; exclude documents not open at publish, report them separately. (4) Placements keep the last applied version and mode; the element shows as deleted; the brand team sees "linked to a deleted element" counts. (5) When the document version syncs; until then the index undercounts, and the answer should state its freshness.

Rubric anchors. 2: a document list on the element, overwritten values. 3: element versions, placements at document-version grain, reverse index, monotonic apply, a stated out-of-date definition. 4: also pending/blocked/kept categories, membership over time, late offline saves, two latency populations, and the incidents handled.

Strong signals. Makes version order the rule for applying updates; separates "can't update" from "hasn't opened". Red flags. Timestamp ordering of updates; arrays of document ids; latency from open documents only, unstated.

ADB-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{as_of}} is the instance's as-of time)

WITH RECURSIVE ev AS (                         -- the books as of the as-of time
  SELECT agreement_id, participant_id, action, delegate_to, occurred_at
  FROM agreement_events
  WHERE occurred_at <= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}'
), open_agreements AS (
  SELECT a.agreement_id, a.sent_at
  FROM agreements a
  WHERE a.signing_order = 'sequential'
    AND a.sent_at <= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}'
    AND (a.cancelled_at IS NULL OR a.cancelled_at > TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}')
    AND (a.expires_at IS NULL OR a.expires_at > TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}')
    AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.agreement_id = a.agreement_id AND ev.action = 'declined')
), chain AS (                                  -- every holder each signer slot has had, in order
  SELECT p.agreement_id, p.step, p.participant_id AS assigned_to, p.participant_id AS holder, 0 AS hops
  FROM agreement_participants p
  JOIN open_agreements o ON o.agreement_id = p.agreement_id
  WHERE p.role = 'signer'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.agreement_id, c.step, c.assigned_to, e.delegate_to, c.hops + 1
  FROM chain c
  JOIN ev e ON e.agreement_id = c.agreement_id AND e.participant_id = c.holder AND e.action = 'delegated'
), slots AS (
  SELECT c.agreement_id, c.step, c.assigned_to,
         (ARRAY_AGG(c.holder ORDER BY c.hops DESC))[1] AS pending_with,
         MIN(s.occurred_at) AS signed_at
  FROM chain c
  LEFT JOIN ev s ON s.agreement_id = c.agreement_id AND s.participant_id = c.holder AND s.action = 'signed'
  GROUP BY c.agreement_id, c.step, c.assigned_to
), current_step AS (
  SELECT agreement_id, MIN(step) AS step
  FROM slots
  WHERE signed_at IS NULL
  GROUP BY agreement_id
), reached AS (
  SELECT cs.agreement_id, cs.step,
         COALESCE((SELECT MAX(s.signed_at) FROM slots s
                   WHERE s.agreement_id = cs.agreement_id AND s.step < cs.step), o.sent_at) AS reached_at
  FROM current_step cs
  JOIN open_agreements o ON o.agreement_id = cs.agreement_id
)
SELECT s.agreement_id, s.step AS current_step, s.assigned_to, s.pending_with,
       ROUND(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}' - r.reached_at) / 3600, 2) AS hours_waiting
FROM slots s
JOIN reached r ON r.agreement_id = s.agreement_id AND r.step = s.step
WHERE s.signed_at IS NULL
ORDER BY hours_waiting DESC, s.agreement_id, s.assigned_to;

Explanation. Everything is rebuilt from events up to the as-of time; the status column is the state at extraction and would drop agreements that were waiting then but finished later. Open agreements are sequential, sent by the as-of time, not cancelled or declined by then (inclusive), and not expired (exclusive: open only while as_of < expires_at). The recursive CTE starts at each signer slot with the named participant as holder and follows delegated events from the current holder, only those at or before the as-of time; the deepest hop is pending_with, and a signed event by any holder in the chain completes the slot (in this data only the final holder signs). The current step is the lowest step with an unsigned slot; the agreement reached it at the latest signature among lower-step slots, or at sent_at when no lower step names a signer (a cc-only step or a gap in the numbering is passed over automatically because only signer slots exist in slots). Delegation never moves the start of the wait. Agreements where every slot is signed have no current step and drop out.

Complexity. One filtered pass over events up to the as-of time, a recursion whose depth is the longest delegation chain (each level a hash join of slots against delegation events), and hash aggregates over slots. The correlated MAX is per open agreement and touches only its slots. In production: partition events by customer and month, keep a per-slot state table (holder, signed_at) maintained from the event stream, and run this as-of logic only for history.

Dialect notes. Snowflake (also CONNECT BY), BigQuery (with an iteration limit) and MySQL 8 support WITH RECURSIVE; recursive CTEs arrived in Databricks SQL only in recent runtimes and older Spark SQL lacks them, where a bounded self-join per hop (chains here are at most two hops) is the fallback (check current docs). (ARRAY_AGG(... ORDER BY ...))[1] is PostgreSQL; use MAX_BY(holder, hops) (Snowflake, Databricks), ARRAY_AGG(holder ORDER BY hops DESC LIMIT 1)[OFFSET(0)] (BigQuery), or a ROW_NUMBER() subquery (MySQL). Hours: DATEDIFF('second', a, b) / 3600 (Snowflake), TIMESTAMP_DIFF(b, a, SECOND) / 3600 (BigQuery), TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, a, b) / 3600 (MySQL); ROUND(x, 2) exists everywhere but float rounding can differ at the last digit. None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. A step signed exactly at the as-of time (the next step is current with 0.00 hours); an agreement cancelled exactly at the as-of time (excluded); a delegation before the as-of time whose delegate signs after it (pending with the delegate, and the extract says completed); a delegation after the as-of time (pending with the named signer); a parallel agreement still in progress (excluded); a draft and an agreement sent after the as-of time (excluded); completed and declined agreements before the as-of time (excluded). Hard adds an agreement expiring exactly at the as-of time (excluded), cc rows next to a signer and cc-only steps (including one at step 1 and one right before the current step), a two-hop delegation chain before the as-of time, a chain whose second hop is after it, and a decline after the as-of time (still waiting). Very Hard adds steps naming two signers (one signed, the other still pending; both pending), and step numbers with gaps.

Common mistakes. Filtering on status; exclusive boundaries; ignoring delegations (pending_with wrong, and the delegate's signature not credited); following delegations after the as-of time; restarting the wait at a delegation; measuring every wait from sent_at; including parallel agreements; ignoring declines; (Hard+) treating cc rows as signers, ignoring expiry or treating expires_at = as_of as open, following only one hop, finding the previous step as current_step - 1; (Very Hard) treating a step as complete when one of its signers has signed. Each has a diagnostic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A cc-only step or a gap: step − 1 has no signer, so a step - 1 join falls back to sent_at and overstates the wait; the data contains such cases from Hard upward. (2) Grain: snapshot date × agreement × slot; rebuild the days on or after the earliest late event's occurred_at (events carry recorded_at to find them). (3) Maintain slot state (current holder, signed_at, became_actionable_at) incrementally from the event stream; a delegation updates one row; history comes from the events. (4) A step becomes a group; waiting rows are all incomplete slots in the lowest incomplete group, and the reached time is the completion of the previous group; the query shape stays the same with set_id in place of step.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but the status column used, or delegations ignored. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains why step − 1 fails, how to snapshot and rebuild after late events, and how slot state would be maintained incrementally.

Strong signals. Asks what the status column reflects before using it; reaches for a recursive CTE for the chain; separates "who holds it" from "how long it has waited". Red flags. WHERE status = 'in_progress'; using MAX(step) + 1 or step - 1 arithmetic for progress; reading document contents or participant emails for a report that needs neither.
